question.leadin: This woman was the last ruler of the Ptolemaic [tall-uh-may-ik] dynasty.
question.text: Name this last queen of independent Egypt before it was conquered by the Romans.
question.clue: Drinking pearls dissolved in vinegar apocryphally won a bet for this ruler, whose short-lived successor was Caesarion.

swap.text: This river has its origins in the Blue and White rivers and, thanks to the Aswan Dam, is not flooding as much as it used to.
swap.clue: The Bari and related peoples migrated up this river after the end of the baqt ("bukt") treaty, which caused kingdoms led from Soba and Dongola to decline and allowed the Funj Sultanate to expand along this river.

question.text: The only remaining wonder of the ancient world is this structure, which was built for Pharaoh Khufu [koo-foo] at Giza.
question.answerHtml: The Great Pyramid of Giza (accept The Great Pyramid of Khufu or reasonable equivalents)
question.clue: Slave labor was long thought to have been used to build this structure, but many archaeologists believe that thousands of skilled laborers were used instead over a 20 year period.

swap.leadin: The Greeks referred to this man as Ozymandias.
swap.text: Name this "great" Egyptian pharaoh who defeated the Nile "Sea People" and claimed a victory at the 1274 BCE Battle of Kadesh.
swap.clue: His refusal to extradite the deposed king Mursili III to Hattusili III led to the signing of the world's first peace treaty.

question.leadin: Limestone blocks known as Talats were used in the construction of a city built by this ruler.
question.text: Name this husband of Nefertiti, a crazy pharaoh who founded a monotheistic religion venerating Aten.
question.clue: This leader created a new capital on the east bank of the Nile, Amarna.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about explorers who weren't from Europe.
swap.text: The ancient Egyptian explorer Neshi was commissioned by this female pharaoh to lead her expedition to Punt. This woman ruled as regent for her son Thutmose III, which stirred his resentment to the point where he tried to erase her from the historical record.
swap.clue: She was the official co-regent of her stepson Thutmose III, who was only two when he came to power and destroyed many images of this ruler after succeeding her.

question.leadin: This city's "Supremacy" over Greece lasted for much of the early 4th century BC.
question.text: Name this central Greek city whose elite troops, the Sacred Band, consisted of 150 pairs of male lovers. It was legendarily the home of King Oedipus and was founded by Cadmus.
question.clue: Troops from this city employed the "cutting off the snake's head" technique to defeat Cleombrotus of Sparta.

swap.leadin: The Sherden pirates may have been one tribe of these people.
swap.text: Name this loose group who frequently attacked ancient Egypt during the collapse of the Bronze Age.
swap.clue: Egypt fought them under Merneptah and Ramses III, and they destroyed the Hittites.

question.leadin: Answer the following about Ancient Egyptian agriculture.
question.text: Irrigation canals were dug in order to control and store the water generated from this annual event. Egyptians would plant their crops in October after the end of this event.
question.answerHtml: flooding of the Nile [or obvious equivalents indicating the overflow or inundation of the Nile River; prompt on floods]

swap.leadin: During a procession honoring this event, Fatimid caliphs would anoint a structure on Roda Island.
swap.text: Name this recurring event. The periods of Peret and Shemu followed this event, which, according to an ancient calendar, occurred during the time of Akhet.
swap.answerHtml: flooding of the Nile River [accepting equivalents for “flooding” like inundation; prompt on flooding with “Of what body of water?”] (The device is the Nilometer.)

question.text: In a Middle Kingdom "tale" titled for this profession, a serpent recounts how a flaming star killed 74 members of his kin. That serpent, who is the Lord of Punt, discusses bravery with a member of this profession.
question.answerHtml: sailor [or al-Baḥriyy; accept The Story of the Shipwrecked Sailor; prompt on merchant]

swap.leadin: Name these Wonders of the Ancient World.
swap.text: Ptolemy I Soter had this structure built by the architect Sostratos on the island of Pharos.
swap.clue: Statues of Arsinoe, along with other parts of this building, were discovered underwater in 1994 by Jean Yves Empereur.

question.text: This group is often credited with introducing chariot warfare to ancient Egypt. This group ruled over the Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt from the city of Avaris.
question.clue: Their capital was at Avaris, and they were overthrown by Ahmose.

swap.text: A Pharaoh's personal name was inscribed inside this symbol, an elongated form of the shen ring motif. This symbol consists of an oval tangent to a straight line.

question.leadin: This figure is depicted on one object preparing to club a figure known as Wash and identified by rebus symbols of a catfish and a chisel.
question.text: Name this ruler depicted on both a namesake macehead and an object used to grind cosmetics, an image that some scholars believe represents the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt.
question.clue: The existence of this pharaoh is attested to by a namesake palette that depicts him with two crowns. This pharaoh was the unifier of Upper and Lower Egypt.

swap.text: Historians often lament the incompleteness of Egyptian king lists, such as the one located in this ancient city's Temple of Seti I. Multiple early dynastic pharaohs were interred in this city's Umm El Qa'ab necropolis.
swap.clue: Nekhen rivaled this city, whose Tomb U-j ("U-J") may house the Predynastic Naqada III ruler King Scorpion I near its tombs of the First Dynasty's Thinite kings.

question.leadin: Answer the following about water in ancient Egypt.
question.text: Two massive statues known by this name were built by Amenhotep III to stand guard over his mortuary temples at the Theban metropolis across the Nile from Luxor. Several projects have been designed around preventing the Nile from eating away at these statues.
question.clue: These are two giant statues of the deified Amenhotep III, one of which depicts his wife Tiy and mother Mutememwia. They flank the entrance of his mortuary temple pylon across the Nile from Luxor.

swap.text: Earlier, this monarch married his sister Arsinoe III, though this notoriously incompetent monarch tried to do away with Theodotus of Aetolia, a man who nobly defend Syria but defected due to poor treatment. Still, he managed to stop Antiochus III of the Seleucids from invading at the Battle of Raphia.

question.text: This man became the third head librarian of the Library around 240 BCE, and he may be best known for developing a namesake "sieve" that identifies prime numbers.
question.clue: To accomplish one of his tasks, this man hired a number of bematists to walk 5,000 stadia.

swap.leadin: An expedition here was reportedly made by the Fifth Dynasty pharaoh Sahure, while later trips were made by Mentuhotep III and finally Ramses III. FTPE.
swap.text: Name this kingdom allegedly in existence from 2500-1170 in Eastern Africa. It's frequently cited as a source of myrrh, ebony, rare wood, and exotic animals like giraffes - as attested by scenes on the temple of Hatshepsut.
swap.clue: A state named in honor of this place was led in the early 20th century by the Warsangali Sultanate and was centered at Garowe.
